newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Zaire elections could be delayed, says official.
newsitem.headline: Zaire elections could be delayed, says official.

text.p: Zaire's first multy-party presidential and parliamentary elections, due by July 1997, may have to be delayed until the end of that year, a senior parliamentary official said on Friday.

"The road is still long and dangerous but I am convinced elections will take place next year, perhaps not as scheduled, but by December 31 at the latest," said Christophe Lutundula Apala Pen' Apala, second vice-president of Zaire's High Council of the Republic -- the transitional government.
According to Zaire's transitional constitution, presidential and parliamentary elections must be held by July 1997.
"But there is a big delay in the calendar for the elections," Lutundula told a conference on Central Africa.
He later told Reuters the delay could be prevented only "if we all get right down to work, at once."

Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko has been under pressure from the United States and European donor countries such as former colonial power Belgium and France to speed up the promised transition to democracy.
Mobutu, who seized power in a 1965 coup, is convalescing in Switzerland after surgery for prostate cancer in late August.
Lutundula said the picture that could be painted of Zaire was a sombre one. He added there was no option but to make the elections successful.
"Otherwise we will enter a turbulent era full of uncertainties."

Lutundula also doubted whether elections could be held in the region of North and South Kivu, which has been swamped by more than two million refugees from neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi following ethnic fighting between Hutus and Tutsis.
"The refugees will not make it easy to hold elections," he said.
"For the moment the two Kivu (provinces) have become a militarised zone...(the situation) could explode any time and set fire to the whole lower region of the Great Lakes," he said.
"That's why the refugees have to return home urgently."
He said he was disappointed that the inernational community played down the problems of refugees in Kivu.
Lutundula, who said Zaire needed a new generation of politicians and leaders, urged opposition parties to refrain from boycotting elections.
"A boycott has never paid off politically. It has never ended a regime and would show the weakness of the opposition. It would be a missed opportunity," he said.
He put the total cost for the elections at $320 million, adding the Zairean government was due to meet a United Nations mission and experts of the European Union soon to decide how to split the bill.
